t: What Building Relationships With Students Really Means ally-means/
q: It’s common for teachers to misunderstand the term “building relationships.
You see, for most students, being cornered into a non-academic conversation with their teacher is uncomfortable—exceedingly so.
Although their heart is in the right place, what develops is a relationship of awkwardness and embarrassment.
But the goal of building relationships with students isn’t familiarity. It’s influence.
If your students trust you because you always do what you say will, and they like you because you’re consistently pleasant, then powerful, behavior-influencing rapport will happen naturally.
Even quiet and shy students—especially quiet and shy students—will come out of the woodwork to laugh and joke with you and exchange goofy smiles.
The fact is, the most effective way to build relationships with students also happens to be the most effective approach to classroom management.

t: Why You Should Avoid Sending Students To The Principal the-principal/
q: Contrary to what many believe, the role of principal doesn’t include directly influencing behavior in your classroom.
When you refer a student to the principal you’re communicating to that student—as well as to the rest of your class—that you’re not the ultimate authority of your classroom.
Relying on your principal to step in and handle what is your responsibility can be devastating to your self-confidence.
The difference is that now they’ll know you’re unable to manage them by yourself—or at all for that matter. Rather than dissuading misbehavior, it emboldens it.

A good principal can have influence on behavior—tremendously so. But it comes indirectly through their leadership, their organizational skills, their expectations of teachers, and their commitment to excellence.
Any dangerous, harmful, or potentially suspendable behavior should be documented and brought to your principal’s attention immediately.
You must show them that you care enough, that they matter enough, for you to be there in the thick of it, right along with them.

t: Why Trial And Error Is Bad For Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/05/17/why-trial-and-error-is-bad-for-difficult-students/
q: They need your fixed boundaries, your steady, predictable presence, your faithful accountability, and your commitment to doing what is right by them and their future.
What they often get, however, is something entirely different. What they often get is an endless succession of haphazard strategies.
One week their every move is corrected . The next week they’re ignored. The week after that they’re excessively praised.
It’s confusing and destructive. It labels them in the eyes of their peers and plays with their emotions.
The fact is, difficult students will never truly improve as long as they’re treated like test subjects. For it isn’t trial and error that transforms behavior.
It’s your fair and consistent accountability. It’s your humor and rapport. It’s the smiles, the gentleness, the mutual likability, and the heartfelt connection between you.
You have to create a stable environment they can count on—one you begin teaching, modeling, and implementing the first day of school .

t: Why Effective Classroom Management Happens Quickly pens-quickly/
q: Classroom management is rarely a slow and steady march to Camelot.
It turns lovely and caring teachers into jaded cynics, filled with resentment and negative thoughts about their class, their school, and their profession.
The upshot is that if your approach to classroom management isn’t working right now, if it isn’t providing the peace and enjoyment you really want, then it’s unlikely to work in the future.
It really is possible to take over any group of students—first day of school, midyear, or otherwise—and transform them into your ideal class.
But if you’re not feeling really good about your class within a week’s time, at most, then it’s a sign you need to make some changes.

As soon as you’re able to unleash the full complement of strategies, as soon as you have a firm grasp of our principles and philosophy, you’ll be able to walk into any teaching situation, no matter how chaotic or unruly, and turn it into the peaceful and fulfilling experience you’ve always longed for.

t: How To Avoid Arguing With Students
q: As soon as you answer back, as soon as you respond and try to justify the consequence, you’re in a full-fledged argument.
You see, the mistake the teacher in the above scenario made was waiting for a response. Many, if not most, teachers do this.
But what this does is invite students to do just that. Before you know it, every time you give a consequence, there is an argument.
Calmly, almost robotically, deliver your consequence and then immediately turn back to what you were doing before .

It’s important to note that how you give a consequence must be thoroughly taught and modeled as part of the series of classroom management-related lessons you’ll teach during the first few weeks of each school year.
In most cases arguing is brought on by the teacher, not the student.
